newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain Supreme Court to rule on "dirty war" files.
newsitem.headline: Spain Supreme Court to rule on "dirty war" files.

text.p: Spain's Supreme Court will decide on Monday whether to insist that the government hand over secret service files on a "dirty war" waged against Basque separatist rebels under the previous Socialist administration.

Lower courts are demanding the declassification of some 20 spy documents that give details of a secret campaign of assassinations and kidnappings against guerrillas of ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) in the 1980s.
But the conservative Popular Party (PP) government has refused, citing reasons of state security.

Documents already leaked to the press suggest the last Socialist government of Felipe Gonzalez was reponsible for organising death squads known as the Anti-Terrorist Liberation Groups (GAL), which killed 28 people between 1983-1987.
Allegations that the Socialists were responsible for setting up the GAL contributed to the election defeat last March of Gonzalez by the PP of Jose Maria Aznar after 13 years in power.

Several former high officials and security chiefs under the Socialist administration have already been charged with involvement in GAL. But the courts complain that evidence is scarce and they need details held in the secret files.

Spanish judges have copies of the documents, which were spirited out of CESID, the country's military intelligence agency. However, the papers are legally worthless unless the government confirms their authenticity by declassifying them.
While Prime Minister Aznar has agreed that the decision should now be left to the judges, Defence Minister Eduardo Serra has said he will defy the Supreme Court if it tries to force the issue.

Supreme Court judges probing the death squads voted six to four last month against questioning Gonzalez, who has consistently denied involvement. But they left the way open to reverse the decision if new evidence emerged.
Last month, two leading Spanish newspapers published leaked papers allegedly stolen from CESID.
The daily El Mundo said the papers directly demonstrated that CESID set up GAL and selected the first victim -- alleged ETA militant Ramon Onederra.

El Pais, which published the entire set of 20 papers, acknowledged that it was not sure if they were authentic, saying they were found during a court search of the prison cell of ex-spy Juan Alberto Perote, who claimed to have stolen them from CESID.
Perote, charged with stealing secret documents, is said to have tried to hide the papers in his prison library and also tried to eat some of them while his cell was being searched.
